doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

chapter: Jazz as a career and wrap-up
title: Should a student go into jazz as a career
summary: Shear advises players to teach, compose and orchestrate too, since pure jazz is very difficult.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Well put. I’m guessing you get this question on occasion, either from a student or maybe from their parents, like gee, do you think I should go into jazz as a career.

I do get that question a lot. But I always say yet but you should be able to teach, you should be able to play, you should be able to compose, you should be able to orchestrate, you should be able to do almost anything you can in music in order to survive and so you won’t have to do anything else. If you just want to be a jazz player and nothing else it’s very difficult. Very, very difficult. There’s a couple of cities only to choose from. And there’s Europe of course, and there’s Asia, particularly Japan, and they love jazz in these places and you could probably make a better living in Europe than the United States. But if you’re going to just be a jazz player, which I have a lot of friends that do want to do that, and they live day to day, month to month, year to year. Most parents don’t want that for their child. Some parents say well whatever makes them happy is fine with me. So it depends on what you want out of life. If you want a family and a nice house and what the American dream used to be or maybe still is, and you just want to play jazz for a living I would say that that’s extremely, extremely difficult.
If you look at some of the — it’s hard to think of a player, a guy like Joe Lovano, they all do other things that come along.
